title: Fire hidden in the wood
hookLine: fire hides in the wood until someone drills for it; the Upanishad says the divine hides in you the same way
carry: god is in you like fire in wood
last: THE SOUL WANDERS WHILE IT FEELS APART.

lines: BACK AND FORTH, UNTIL IT SMOKES.
cards: Before matches, a Vedic priest made the sacred fire from two pieces of wood: a flat lower block and a pointed upper stick.
He set the stick in a notch, wrapped a cord around it, and pulled, back and forth, until the wood smoked and a coal glowed. The two sticks were called the arani.
Every household fire in the old rites began that way, with friction and patience. Hold that picture, because the Shvetashvatara is about to say that you are the wood.

teach.h: THE FIRE HIDES, BUT ISN'T LOST.
teach.b: Verse 1.13, in paraphrase: the form of fire hidden in its source isn't seen, and yet it isn't destroyed. It can be caught again from the wood by drilling.
In the same way, the self is caught in the body by om. Then verse 1.14 builds the whole fire kit. Make your own body the lower stick, and the sacred syllable om the upper.
By the churning of meditation, you will see God, like fire hidden in the wood. The word for that drilling is related to churning, the same motion as churning butter out of milk.

teach.h: OIL IN SESAME, BUTTER IN CREAM.
teach.b: The next verses keep going: like oil in sesame seeds, butter in cream, water in a dry riverbed, fire in the fire sticks, the self is found within by one who seeks it with truth and discipline.
Here's the teaching, plainly, and it runs all through Hinduism: God isn't missing. God is already within you, hidden, undamaged. What's missing is friction, repeated and patient.

teach.h: GOD IS IN YOU LIKE FIRE IN WOOD.
teach.b: One pull of the cord does nothing. A hundred pulls, and there's smoke.
That's why so many Hindus repeat om or a mantra every day, often on a mala of a hundred and eight beads: not to make God appear, but to keep the drill turning until something kindles.

how: In Vedic ritual the sacred fire is still kindled by drilling the arani fire sticks at some major rites, and many Hindus who meditate use om, silently or aloud, as the steady repetition the Upanishad describes.

o: the fire sticks, rubbed together to kindle fire
the ladle used to pour butter into the fire
the clay altar where the sacred fire is kept

games.q: the fire kit of 1.14: tap the pairs.

s: the verse says the fire is missing until meditation creates it
1.13 says the fire hidden in the wood isn't seen, but isn't destroyed. it is already there.
the Upanishad compares the hidden self to oil in sesame seeds
and butter in cream, water in a dry riverbed, fire in the fire sticks (1.15).
the arani were two pieces of wood used to make the sacred fire
a lower block and an upper drill, worked back and forth.

games.q: you've drilled the fire sticks a dozen times and seen no smoke. what does the Upanishad's picture suggest?
o: the wood has no fire in it.
keep churning: the fire is there, it takes repeated friction.
throw the sticks away and wait for lightning.
games.why: the verses insist the fire is hidden, not absent. it is caught by drilling, by the practice of churning, which the text calls meditation.

practice: Feel the weight of your body, the lower stick, and on each out-breath let a long, quiet om sound, inside or aloud, the upper stick.
Don't look for sparks; just keep the gentle back and forth going, the way the old priests kept the cord moving. When attention wanders, that's one pull of the cord: come back and pull again.

wordCard.voice: Arani, the fire-drilling sticks. The Shvetashvatara's picture of practice: the body as one stick, om as the other, and steady churning until the hidden fire shows.

orig.note: Sanskrit araṇi: the fire-drilling sticks of Vedic ritual. in 1.14 the body is the lower one, om the upper.
